Welcome from Head of School
Original handbook page
Dear Oaks Christian Parents and Students,
Welcome to the 2026-2027 school year! We are excited to have you at Oaks and count it a significant
privilege to be able to partner with you in your educational journey and in our mission of “preparing minds for
leadership and hearts for service.”
We have compiled this handbook to provide an expression of our expectations of each other as a learning
community. Its content spans from issues of academic concerns to student life to parent involvement.
Although the school has prepared this handbook with careful and thoughtful planning, no doubt there will be
additional issues and unforeseen concerns as we walk through this school year together. When this
happens, we will do our best to communicate with you clearly and quickly, as may be appropriate. In addition
to this document, we have made a digital version of the High School Campus Handbook available on AXIS
so that parents and students may access it, if needed, at any time.
As this handbook seeks to address most of the general parameters of school life at OCS, it is important that
every parent and student read the entire handbook to become familiar with its content and expectations.
Students and parents are responsible for understanding the procedures and policy guidelines outlined in this
handbook. Completing the enrollment process indicates that the handbook was read, understood, and
agreed to for compliance. Information, policies, procedures, and guidelines are an attempt to help the
community operate smoothly and fairly, while allowing for discretion, discernment, wisdom and grace within
these boundaries, parameters, and guidelines to be considered and enjoyed. The spirit of this handbook is to
allow OCS to conduct itself in such a way as to give glory and honor to God, and dignity to each other, in a
compassionate and caring way. Our expectation is that our students will use appropriate and proper
judgment when given responsibility. It is with that explicit and heartfelt desire that we offer this handbook to
the school community.
The student community has a unique opportunity and responsibility to set the standard, and impact the
culture, of the school for the future. OCS students will determine school pride and spirit; academic, artistic,
and athletic reputation; spiritual development and leadership; and service to the surrounding community. The
tradition of Oaks Christian continues with you. May you carry the mantle forward in such a manner that well
represents yourself, your family, and your school.
Blessings,
Robert T. Black
Head of School/President

Crest
About our Crest: The Oaks Christian School crest was designed in 2009 by alum Chris Thompson. The
symbols, colors and phrases were chosen to symbolize the values of the OCS mission statement. The crest
is a shield, chosen as a reflection of the shield of faith as articulated in Ephesians 6:13-17. Key words from
the Oaks Christian School mission statement, translated into Latin, border the shield: Erudita Prudentia
(Academic Excellence), Claritas Artium (Artistic Expression), Insignis Athletica (Athletic Distinction).
The deatils of the crest represent the following ideas:
Cross—represents Christ, Christianity, and Christian service.
Acorn—represents antiquity, strength, and continuous growth.
Bible/Book—represents God’s Word and its timeless truths.
Keys—represents unlocking, opening, explaining, and freedom.

Olive Branches—represents peace, concordance, and harmony.

Educational Philosophy and Goals
Educational Philosophy
Oaks Christian School exists to provide a Christ-centered education founded on a biblical worldview that
honors God and ensures every student can acquire the knowledge and character necessary for progressive
growth. This is expressed in the following pursuits:
We aspire to instill in our students a passion to love God and others, demonstrated through virtues such as
integrity, discernment, compassion, leadership, and joy. In this, students care for themselves and each other.
We value the uniqueness of each student and seek to both know them and support their progress as
scholars, artists, and athletes in its varied and individual expression.
We create a diverse, challenging learning environment that draws students away from self-centered thinking
to active contribution. When students encounter struggle, rather than shy away, they learn to persist in
problem-solving by drawing on the curiosity, character, and understanding cultivated through their studies.
They engage in ideas that prepare them to meet the challenges of their world and make a positive difference.
We desire a community of servant-leaders who through wisdom and love desire to bring good to the world.
School Goals
The Oaks Christian Community will
foster an understanding of the sovereignty of God, which provides a framework for the application of
knowledge;
provide a comprehensive and college preparatory education through diverse learning experiences within
an engaging community;
provide a challenging learning environment that fosters critical thinking, personal responsibility, and
persistent effort;
refine our bodies and character through teamwork and in competition that honors God;
develop an understanding and appreciation of the arts, and encourage good stewardship of our artistic
abilities;
encourage a passion to love God and others through living lives that reflect the virtues taught and
modeled by Christ including justice, wisdom, courage, service, reconciliation, grace, and humility.

OCS Social Media Policy—Students and Parents
Oaks Christian School and Social Media
Today’s world offers constant and dynamic communication. Navigating it responsibly and productively is our
goal at Oaks Christian School.
As a school, we value the emergence of social media as a communication tool and one which affords us the
opportunity to communicate on a daily and interactive basis through our official Facebook, Twitter, and
Instagram platforms. While we value social media, we caution our parents and students to understand the
benefits and dangers of its use.
On the pages that follow, please find the OCS Social Media Policy and associated protocols, which have
been established for the protection of Oaks Christian School, employees, students, and parents from private
and unprofessional uses of social media, as well as to maintain consistent communication opportunities for
OCS students who may not be allowed access to social media platforms. Please keep in mind that it is not
the school’s desire to limit effective and necessary communications, but to put reasonable, responsible, and
professional protocols in place for the protection of the OCS community and to uphold Oaks Christian
School’s quality standards.
OCS Social Media Policy—Students and Parents
Vision and Mission: At Oaks Christian School, our vision is to allow the official OCS social media platforms to
be an extension of our school website and AXIS (Learning Management System) providing a dynamic venue
for students, parents, and friends to receive up-to-date event information and news about OCS students and
the OCS community at large, while advancing our school mission for “academic excellence, artistic
expression, athletic distinction.” For example, our official Oaks Christian School Facebook provides a day-to-
day view into OCS student life as we post photos and news about student academic, artistic, athletic,
spiritual life, and community service accomplishments. Our official sites are carefully managed by designated
OCS employees, ensuring consistency in professionalism, integrity, privacy standards, and accuracy of the
information.
Unauthorized Sites: Unfortunately, there have been unsanctioned social media sites that have used the Oaks
Christian School name, word marks, and logos, while violating trademark laws and misrepresenting our
school. These unauthorized sites have the potential to promote cyberbullying, harassment, and other unsafe
or unlawful practices, and every effort is made to close these sites. Please visit only the authorized, official
OCS Facebook, Twitter and Instagram sites when connecting to Oaks Christian School via social media.
Official OCS Social Media Sites: Official OCS social media sites are managed under the oversight of the
marketing department. The school’s official OCS social media accounts are listed below. To maintain and

children and keep aware of the constantly changing climate of social media.

Biblical Worldview
Original handbook page
Statement of Faith
All people in all places hold presuppositions around which they order their very existence. A worldview is a
perspective, a set of precepts that guides our behavior, a way of thinking and doing. A Biblical worldview is
one built on the premise that all truth is God’s truth. Thus, if God is the Sovereign Creator, then all areas of
inquiry are beneficial for our edification. This translates into a desire to know, a thirst to understand humanity
and the world. The facts upon which Christianity rest, as found in the scriptures and Christian doctrines,
inform and make up the framework of the Biblical worldview.
At Oaks Christian School, denominational differences are to be understood, while the essentials of the faith
are to be celebrated. We look at all of learning and life through the following truths of scripture:
Creation (humanity made in God’s image; creation is good; innate desire to know God’s sovereignty)
The Fall (sin and its effects; death; humanity’s constant struggle with God)
Redemption (of humanity back to God; the incarnation of God in Christ; salvation)
Future Hope (eternity; the temporal versus eternal world; the Second Coming of Christ)
We recognize the common grace (revelation of the truths of God to Christians and non-Christians alike)
manifested throughout all the created order.
Statement of Faith
We believe the Bible to be the inspired and only infallible Word of God.
We believe that there is only one God, eternally existent in three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
We believe that mankind was created good, but lost the hope of life eternal, destroyed his communion
with God, and fell under the bondage of sin and death by rebelling against God’s perfect way of life.
We believe that Jesus Christ is God’s eternal Son, who redeemed mankind. As true God and true man,
He was born of a virgin through the Holy Spirit, taught men how to live through His sinless life, took the
consequences of our sin upon Himself in His passion and death upon the cross, arose bodily from the
dead on the third day after His death, was seen by His disciples, ascended to the right hand of the
Father and will return in power and glory.
We believe that all are sinners, that all are called to repentance and faith in Jesus Christ, that no one can
come to the Father except through Jesus Christ, and that no one can come to faith in Christ, repent and
attain holiness, but by the grace of God.
We believe as a gift from God, sexual intimacy is to be experienced only between a man and a woman
within a marital relationship. We believe, therefore, that any other form of sexual intimacy is not in
keeping with God’s plan for mankind.
We believe that the Holy Spirit is freely given to those that believe in Jesus Christ, that the fruits and
benefits of Christ’s redemption are applied to us individually by the Holy Spirit, and that the Holy Spirit

lives in us and enables us to live godly lives.
We believe that at the end of the age there will be two resurrections: one to eternal life and glory, the

Graduation Requirements and General
Policies
Original handbook page
ACADEMIC REQUIREMENTS
ACADEMIC LIFE
Students at Oaks Christian School are developing the ability to think critically and deeply; preparing for
college; becoming independent and articulate learners; forming within themselves the knowledge and
responsibility for leadership; seeking to develop their faith; and developing a sense of a Christian worldview.
Essential to this are supportive teachers—dedicated Christians who are excellent both in teaching and in
knowledge. Teachers do not separate intellectual life from the spiritual. In the academic environment at Oaks
Christian School, students will be challenged to think independently, open-mindedly, critically, and creatively.
But it is also integral to our mission that students will be challenged to know God. All disciplines emphasize
critical thinking, formulation and defense of ideas, and the presentation of facts. To this end, effective writing
is stressed in instruction across disciplines, and it is not uncommon for a course to be taught in a seminar
format. The Oaks Christian School course of study requires students to read extensively and to be highly
motivated.
ACADEMIC REQUIREMENTS
Requirements for Promotion and Diploma—The following pertain to the granting of promotion and diplomas:
To be promoted and eligible for a diploma, a student must earn credit in all graduation requirements
outlined below.
A failing grade in a course that is not required for graduation will be recorded but will not jeopardize
eligibility for a diploma.
Seniors who have failed one or more of the required academic classes, or another requirement such as
PE, will be required to repeat the failed work in an accredited summer school before receiving a diploma
or a transcript showing the graduation date.
Diploma Requirements—The curriculum of Oaks Christian School is college-preparatory. It comprises a
required core of studies believed to be fundamental to a liberal arts education as well as elective courses
designed to fit the needs and interests of the individual student. The course of study follows a traditional
college-preparatory path, which includes advanced offerings. For a four-year program at Oaks Christian
School, a minimum of 21 academic credits is required for graduation: Bible (2.5 years); history (3.5 years);
English (4 years); mathematics (3 years—must successfully complete Algebra II); science (3 years—must
complete biology and either chemistry or physics); foreign language (must complete either Level III or two
years of two separate languages); fine arts (2 years—one credit must include a continuous, year-long class).
Other requirements include two credits in PE (see below for details), one half-credit semester elective, one-
Oaks Christian School • High School Student Handbook — 26 / 92

year elective credit in Health, and community service. All graduation requirements must be taken through
Oaks Christian School.
Physical Education—Each student is required to take any combination of two semesters of PE or seasons of
participation on an OCS athletic team. Although we encourage students to try out for athletic teams, we
cannot guarantee each student a place on the team. If a student is cut from a team or chooses not to
participate, s/he can enroll in an independent physical education course through Oaks Christian Online
School.
Summer School—Many students attend summer school for enrichment, remediation, or advancement.
Except when making up a D or F in a class required for graduation, Oaks Christian School does not give
course credit for summer study taken outside of Oaks Christian School, although placement credit may be
given. For continuity, Oaks Christian School recommends remediation or advancement courses be taken
through our summer school whenever possible. Summer school grades from outside of Oaks Christian
School appear on the OCS transcript but are not calculated in the student’s Oaks Christian School GPA
although it can positively affect college admissions, CIF, and graduation eligibility. Oaks Christian School
summer school grades replace the original grade for the purpose of GPA calculation, but the original grade
will remain, along with the new grade, on the transcript. Students who wish to improve a grade of C- or lower
may do so at a community college or other accredited institution, or they may retake the course during the
regular school year. The original course taken at Oaks Christian School, however, remains in the student’s
GPA. Students taking summer school courses to advance to a higher level in any discipline must discuss the
plan with the appropriate department chair during the spring semester prior to summer school enrollment.
The department chair may arrange an Oaks Christian School examination at the end of the summer. If work
on the examination shows that the student is prepared for the next level, his/her schedule will be changed
accordingly.
GPA—A weighted GPA is used to determine NHS (National Honor Society) eligibility, valedictorian, “Top Ten”
honors, and limited other recognitions.
Valedictorian- The student with the highest weighted GPA (based on 7 semesters) in the graduating class is
eligible to be valedictorian. However, the awarding of this distinction is subject to approval from the Director
of College Counseling, Senior Academic Dean, High School Principal, and ultimately, the Head of School.
Students with academic concerns not directly reflected in a GPA may still be ruled ineligible to earn the
distinction of valedictorian. Examples of concerns are listed below. This is not an all-inclusive list.
Academic Integrity violations or concerns
Behavior concerns in and out of the classroom
Disingenuous college admissions processes
Additionally, the distinction of valedictorian does not ensure a speaking role at graduation. The student
speakers at graduation are based on student nominations and administrative approval.
ACADEMIC LIFE
Daily Schedule—Classes rotate through a modified block schedule. Students meet with all their classes on
Anchor Days (typically Mondays) and then rotate through their classes on alternating A Days (typically
Oaks Christian School • High School Student Handbook — 27 / 92

Tuesdays/Thursdays) and B Days (typically Wednesdays/Fridays). Schedules are updated and accurate in
AXIS and should be checked regularly.
Class Load—Freshmen and Sophomores are expected to take seven classes. Juniors are expected to take a
minimum of six classes. Seniors are expected to take a minimum of five classes. This total includes classes
taken on campus and through OCO.
Open Periods—Some students may not be scheduled for a formal class during one of the class rotations.
Because of the academic expectations of the school, students are expected to use their time appropriately.
Open periods are for on-campus tutoring, meeting teachers, participating in study groups, or other
responsible uses. A student’s priority is always to make up for any deficiency in a class.
Textbooks—Oaks Christian provides book purchasing services through AXIS in our online bookstore. The
Oaks Christian Bookstore provides purchasing choices for all required texts, both digital and print. Please
purchase all required texts well in advance to avoid backorders or expedited shipping fees. These texts must
be purchased in advance as students will use the first days of school. Teachers will provide other resources
in class or if necessary, additional purchasing information for supplies.
Homework—Successful instruction depends on the preparation of each student. Students are expected to
enter class prepared with the previously assigned work. The amount will vary from assignment to assignment
and some upper-level honors/AP courses may require more time.
Late Work—Meeting deadlines by turning assigned work in on time provides check points for growth and
builds foundations for future learning. Whether late work can be turned in after a unit has passed is subject to
department policy (found in course syllabus). However, work from the previous quarter cannot be turned in
during the new quarter. Any exception must be approved by the high school principal.
Make-up Work—Students are expected to complete assignments on time and to take tests and quizzes when
assigned. Students must make up work immediately upon missing school, no later than the day after
returning to school, unless the absence is prolonged and/or arrangements have been made with the teacher.
Students who miss class because of any school function (e.g., athletics, trips, and school business) must
make up the work no later than the next school day. The school does not ask teachers to accept late work. If
such work is accepted, it will be assessed with a penalty per dept policy.
A student who misses a single class period or part of the day is required to make up any quizzes/tests and
turn in any assignments due on the same day of the partial absence.
A student who misses class the day before a test or the day of the test is expected to take the test
immediately upon returning to school.
Students who are called out for an appointment and do not pre-arrange a time to make up the assessment
with the teacher will be assessed a grade penalty.
Concussion Protocol
If a student suffers a head injury or is suspected of suffering from a concussion, the nurse or trainer will
require the student to be evaluated by a licensed health professional who is qualified to diagnose
concussions.
It is the responsibility of the student to report to the school if he/she has been diagnosed with a concussion,
whether the concussion occurred at school or off campus.
Oaks Christian School • High School Student Handbook — 28 / 92

If a student is diagnosed with a concussion, then academic accommodation may be provided pending
documentation from the licensed health professional. The preferred form of documentation is through an
ACE form.
The school nurse will receive all medical documentation and then contact the Academic Dean who will
communicate with the teachers of the student. Students who are on academic accommodations may not
“Return to Play” in any extracurricular activity (sports, dance, and performances) until a clearance has been
submitted with both “Return to Play” and “Return to Learn.” In other words, a student is not allowed to be
playing an Oaks sport/performing at Oaks if the student is still on academic accommodations.
Students who are suffering from a concussion for an extended period may be required to have periodic follow
ups with their health professional accompanied by follow up documentation. In rare cases, students out for a
prolonged period may need to take an incomplete in the course and complete the course(s) by an agreed
upon time period.
Final Exams—Two-hour examinations are given at the end of each semester and are required for most
courses. The grade received is incorporated into the semester grade and can be no more than 20% of that
grade.
Rescheduling Final Exams—Students who cannot take their final exam at the given time must submit a
request to reschedule a final examination at least two weeks in advance to the Office of Academics. Upon
review, the Dean will determine if the final can be rescheduled and if any grade deduction will be taken from
the final score. Parents are required to schedule their vacations around exam schedules. Please contact the
Office of Academics with questions, 818.575.9236.
Honors/Advanced Placement Programs—The Honors and AP programs offer enrichment in which learning is
done at greater depth and at a faster pace. The student in such a class is an accomplished reader and a
skilled, analytical thinker. Each honors and AP course has specific prerequisites and necessary approvals to
enroll or stay in the program. Students may only take three such courses unless petition for four is granted by
the Academic Office. Faculty may recommend that a student be dropped if it becomes clear early in the year

Academic integrity is honesty in a scholastic environment. It is a particularly important part of the educational
process at Oaks Christian School. Academic integrity is a key component of a student’s moral character and
is essential for the development of the whole person within a Christian learning environment. Academic
integrity is also a key component of the entire school’s moral character and is essential for the development
of an academic climate of mutual trust and of a spiritual community where honesty and respect prevail.
Academic integrity needs to be upheld by students and staff alike, and how well this is done will determine
the quality of students who attend Oaks Christian School, now and in the future.
The following Academic Integrity Code clearly defines plagiarism, cheating, facilitation of academic
dishonesty, fabrication, and violation of U.S. copyright laws. These definitions provide a framework for the
training of the students and faculty so that all may glorify God through their academic work. The Academic
Integrity Code also describes the clear-cut procedures and consequences that should result if intentional acts
of dishonesty occur.
Why Academic Integrity Matters
The necessity of students doing their own work is an inherent part of classroom protocol and instruction.
Teachers, advisors, and administration provide training and clarification for students both formally and
informally through academic assemblies, freshmen adviory tech conversations, day-to-day lessons and
assesments. The goal is not to police behavior but to shape character based on the understanding that how
we learn is as important as what we learn.
Definitions of Academic Dishonesty
Plagiarism is the unacknowledged use of another’s words or ideas (from the Latin word, plagiarius, which
means “kidnapper”). This happens in many forms including but not limited to:
Omitting a source citation for another’s idea or failing to include a bibliography or works cited page
when requested for an assignment.
Copying directly from a source when you mean to paraphrase.
Neglecting to place quotation marks around another writer’s words.
Putting your name on a group project in which others in the group have done most or all the work.
Oaks Christian School • High School Student Handbook — 36 / 92

Claiming significant portions of text as your own when they are in fact copied from a source.
Summarizing or paraphrasing another’s idea, thought, or concept without acknowledging the source.
Cheating is the use of unauthorized materials, information, or study aids in an academic exercise.
Cheating can also be a secret agreement made among students in visual or oral form for fraudulent
purposes.
Copying or receiving an answer on an assessment (e.g., test, quiz, or any other coursework that is
evaluated by your teacher).
Using any unauthorized source of information during an assessment.
Acquiring specific knowledge of the content of an assessment before it is given.
Illegally obtaining a copy of an assessment before it is given.
Changing an answer on a graded assessment and then claiming the teacher made a grading error.
Copying homework or other class work.
Using a paper, in whole or part, written by another person.
Submitting the same work or major portions of the same work for two classes without permission.
Using an on-line translator for foreign language classes.
Facilitating academic dishonesty occurs when one student knowingly or negligently aids others or allows
his or her work to be used in a dishonest academic manner. Such students are equally as guilty of an
academic integrity violation as the recipients of their aid.
Not reporting knowledge of a violation of the Academic Integrity.
Providing false or misleading information during an investigation of a possible Academic Integrity
violation.
Allowing another person to copy homework or other class work.
Not preventing your work from being easily seen or copied by another student or copied during an
assessment.
Verbally, visually, or in writing helping another person during an assessment.
Accepting, sharing, or distributing a copy of an assessment before it is given.
Accepting, sharing, or distributing knowledge of an assessment before it is given.
Providing a student with an assessment or completed assignment from a previous semester or year.
Fabrication is the exaggeration or falsification of research data or survey results.
Including data collected or generated by another person in any portion of a report related to a laboratory
or classroom activity.
Presenting data that does not accurately reflect your actual results in any portion of a report related to a
laboratory or classroom activity.
Creating or modifying data to support any interpretations or conclusions more strongly in any portion of
a report related to a laboratory or classroom activity.
The use of artificial intelligence (chatGPT, Photomath, Google translate, Calculator, etc.) is not allowed
to be presented as authentic work without teacher approval. Any use of such software will be treated as
a violation of our academic integrity code outlined by the process below.

Violation of U.S. Copyright Law occurs when a person copies, creates, or uses unauthorized copies of
software, videos, songs, or printed materials that are copyrighted or trademarked. Limited use of these
materials in an educational setting is allowed provided it includes full copyright information and follows all
other guidelines set forth by U.S. Copyright Law. More information can be found at www.copyright.gov for

Using an image from a print or electronic source as part of your work without providing full copyright

Using an icon, character, name, phrase, or slogan, or any other trademarked material without including

If a faculty member suspects a student dishonesty, s/he should first meet with the student, discuss the

detailed explanation of the offense and a summary of the conversation with the student. The Senior
Academic Dean will follow-up with the student and assign appropriate consequeces.

Overview
The administration, faculty and staff of Oaks Christian School are committed to providing an exemplary
education in a safe environment. The guiding principles for conduct at Oaks Christian School are found in the
words of Christ in the gospel of Mark 12 regarding love: “Love your neighbor as yourself,” and Matthew 18
regarding reconciliation: “If your brother sins against you, go and show him his fault, just between the two of
you.” Members of the Oaks Christian School community treat each other with respect, dignity, and kindness.
Led by the Deans of Student Life, Oaks Christian School will work with parents during the discipline process.
Students who are unable to meet the student conduct standards set by the school will not be able to remain
at Oaks Christian School. The key aspect of this process is finding students that best fit the mission and
goals of the school. The admission process affords the school this important distinctive. Oaks Christian
School believes that students enter school for serious reasons and that, in general, their consciences and
Oaks Christian School • High School Student Handbook — 49 / 92

common sense are sufficient guides for their behavior. A sense of responsibility for one’s own conduct as well
as for the general well-being of the community is expected.
Any discussion of discipline must begin with self-discipline. The teachings of Paul, found in Galatians 5,
regarding the Spirit-controlled life and the teaching in James 3 regarding how we speak, stress the
importance of self-control. As students mature, they become less dependent on rules to govern their
behavior, and more dependent on their own ability to do what is right. Our process, then, is based upon the
personal integrity of students and their willingness to practice self-control. When there is a breakdown in self-
discipline, peer discipline becomes important. It is crucial that friendships at our school include the
willingness to confront each other in love, and thus be responsible for each other’s growth in this way.
School personnel need to apply community discipline when a student exercises poor judgment, is
uncooperative, or is disruptive in some way. In the classroom, teachers are responsible for maintaining the
control and discipline necessary to establish a quality learning environment. The deans of student life, vice-
principal, principal, and head of school support the teacher in this disciplinary role and will become involved
whenever student disruption and lack of cooperation warrant their attention and sanction. Teachers are
encouraged to be consistent in their disciplinary actions and to keep the discipline in line with the offense,
with the goal in mind of helping students to move towards self-discipline. When appropriate, a student’s
advisor may be involved in the resolution process. The deans of student life, vice-principal, principal and the
head of school will consult, as appropriate, on all disciplinary actions taken. The head of school shall have
the final decision on all disciplinary actions. The goal of the discipline process is reconciliation and
redemption. The Oaks Christian School community is encouraged to resolve matters quickly and properly.
Before students can attend classes, they and their parents are required to sign off electronically on the High
School Campus Handbook, agreeing to abide by all policies in the Campus Handbook as implemented by
the administration, faculty, and staff of Oaks Christian School. Attendance by a student shall be deemed an
agreement by the students and their parents that they have reviewed the Campus Handbook and agree to
abide by all OCS policies.

Christian School community.

Absolute respect for the rights of others is expected of all members of the school community. Academic

library, or in the lunch area, will not be tolerated. Rudeness, profanity, socially offensive language, or
malicious behavior (physical or verbal) to faculty, staff, or peers will not be tolerated. Students involved in
fighting are subject to suspension or dismissal from school, in the sole and absolute discretion of the school.
Dishonesty, lying, insolence, profanity, verbal abuse, hectoring, unlawful harassment (including sexual

Students are not permitted to use rideshare services, taxis, or similar transportation providers to leave
campus during the school day. Once a student arrives on campus, they must remain on campus until
dismissal unless signed out by a parent/guardian or an authorized emergency contact. The School will not
release students to rideshare drivers or other third-party transportation providers on campus. Any student
who leaves campus without authorization is considered off campus without permission and will be subject to
disciplinary action.
Lanyard Policy
As a safety precaution, all high school students must wear their lanyard and school identification around their
neck while on campus, including open periods. Lanyards must always be worn around the neck and visible
(not under jackets or polos). Students found without their school ID’s will be directed to the Office of Student
Life for disciplinary action (see below). If a student comes to school without their lanyard, they will be sent to
the Office of Student Life for a temporary badge and disciplinary action. Students will be provided with an ID
card and lanyard at the beginning of the year. Students are only allowed to wear school approved/provided
lanyards. The replacement fee is $10.00, $5.00 fee to replace student identification cards and a $5.00 fee to
replace lanyards, cash only.
As the campus continues to grow and hosts numerous guests, events, and special programs throughout the
year, visible identification provides an additional layer of security without
significantly impacting the student experience. A lanyard system allows staff to quickly identify individuals
who may not belong on campus, supports faster and more accurate responses during emergencies, and
reduces the need for staff to repeatedly stop students to verify their identity. The purpose of visible
identification is to promote a safe, secure, and welcoming learning environment where students can flourish.
Consequences (Per Year):
The entire Oaks Christian School community, including faculty, staff, parents, and students, is responsible for
making sure that students follow the safety and security guidelines set by the school. Students who do not
follow the school guidelines will be sent to the Office of Student Life and will be required to have a lanyard
before returning to class. Repeated violations of the uniform will result in consequences (see below). Each
offense will be recorded in AXIS under the student’s conduct section.

notified. Students will need to return this badge at the end of the day. If student has lost badge and
lanyard, they will need to pay the replacement fee of $10. Parent(s) will receive an automated message.

Transportation
Parents and students are to follow the policies and procedures regarding transportation to and from school,
either by private transportation or by transportation arranged by the school. Students who travel on a school
bus or other means of transportation during a school activity are to follow the rules that they are given at that
time.
Student Parking/Automobiles
Students who drive to school are to follow the proper traffic flow and procedures. Students are to park in the
areas designated for student parking. Students who are interested in parking on campus need to obtain
approval by filling out the proper paperwork from the Office of Student Life and receiving a parking pass. This
pass shall be always visible while the vehicle is parked on campus. Students are not allowed in the student
parking area during school hours, except when they are arriving or leaving school, unless granted written
permission from the Office of Student Life. Students are to use their student lockers for those items they will
need during the school day. Students who do not park in the designated student parking area, who do not
follow the proper traffic flow, who do not have permission to be in the student parking area or who do not
drive in a safe and responsible manner may have their parking privileges suspended or revoked. Any student
parking a vehicle on campus, or on the street outside of campus, agrees that school personnel have the right
to search the vehicle at any time during school hours or during any school activity and student agrees to fully
cooperate in providing access to the vehicle upon request by school personnel. Failure of a student to
cooperate upon request shall subject the student to disciplinary action, at the sole discretion of the school,
including, but not limited to dismissal.
Bikes, Skateboards, etc.

Students who ride a bike to school must secure their bike to the bike rack. Skateboarding or rollerblading on
school property is not allowed at any time. Students who bring skateboards, roller blades and/or other such
items to school are to store them with the Office of Student Life.
Hoverboards
Students must abide by the state and local laws regarding hoverboards (Assembly Bill 604). Hoverboards
are not allowed to be brought, used, or stored on campus due to safety reasons. Hoverboards will be
confiscated and released to parents only.
Distribution and posting of information
Persons interested in distributing or posting any information (school and non-school related) on school
property must obtain prior approval in writing from the Office of the Head of School or the Office of Student
Life. Materials are to be posted in designated spaces (as approved by the Office of Student Life) and not on
windows or doors.
Lockers
Students will be issued lockers at the beginning of their freshman year by the attendance office and expected
to abide by the following rules:
In the interest of safety and to ensure compliance with school policies prohibiting the presence of drugs,
alcohol, weapons, and contraband, Oaks Christian School reserves the right to inspect lockers and their
contents without prior notice or cause.
The lockers should be kept neat and treated properly. Lockers may be decorated on the inside if done
appropriately, but the school reserves the right to require students to remove decorations that are
inappropriate. Lockers may not be decorated on the outside except when done for birthdays or other
special occasions. These decorations must be ones that can be easily removed by the student at the
end of the day. Balloons, crepe paper, and streamers are acceptable, but no glitter, confetti, stickers, or
paint allowed.
Students may access their lockers during any unscheduled period or with teacher permission.
Students are encouraged to keep valuables locked in their lockers or in their possession at all times.
Students are not to share their locker or the combination to their locker with anyone.
Lost and found
All articles left on campus, except athletic articles, which will be placed in the lost and found boxes in the
locker rooms, will be placed in the lost and found located on the racks on the second floor. Please mark all
articles belonging to you with your name and check for any lost item as soon as it is missing. On the last
Friday of every month, we will collect all the lost and found items. Labeled items will be made available for
retrieval for one extra week. After that time, the name will be removed, and the item will be placed in
Malachi’s closet or donated to the Rescue Mission.
